title: Jack Jouett, Kentucky’s midnight rider
summary: In June 1781 Jack Jouett rode about forty miles to warn Jefferson of British cavalry, then moved to Kentucky to farm and serve as a legislator.
bodyMarkdown:
On the night of June 3–4, 1781, Capt. John "Jack" Jouett Jr., a 26-year-old Virginia militia officer, was at Cuckoo Tavern in Louisa County when he saw [Banastre Tarleton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Banastre_Tarleton)'s British raiders pass. The column of about 180 dragoons and 70 mounted infantry was riding to capture Governor [Thomas Jefferson](https://grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Jefferson) and the Virginia legislature at Charlottesville. Jouett guessed their target and set out to beat them there.

He avoided the main road, where British scouts might catch him, and rode about forty miles through woods and back trails. He reached [Monticello](https://grokipedia.com/page/Monticello) near dawn and then warned the legislators in town. Most of the government escaped.

Virginia voted Jouett a pair of pistols and a sword for the ride. He received the pistols in 1783. The record of the sword is less clear.

[Jouett](https://grokipedia.com/page/Jack_Jouett) moved west in 1782 to the part of Virginia that became Kentucky, settling first in what became [Mercer County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mercer_County,_Kentucky). In 1784 he married Sally (Sarah) Robards. Lincoln County voters sent him to the Virginia House of Delegates, where he backed separate statehood for Kentucky.

After 1792 he served in the Kentucky House, first for Mercer and later for [Woodford County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Woodford_County,_Kentucky). On a 530-acre Woodford farm, near Craig's Creek outside [Versailles](/stories/versailles-takes-shape/), he built a brick house about 1797. He improved livestock with imported cattle and horses and ran a grist mill and a distillery.

Jouett's life followed a path many Revolutionary veterans took. Wartime service brought standing at home, and that standing helped him win land and office on the frontier. The farms and stations of such men pushed Kentucky settlement onto land that Shawnee, Cherokee and other nations still contested in those years.

He died on March 1, 1822, in [Bath County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bath_County,_Kentucky).

## Kentucky today

The Jack Jouett House Historic Site near Versailles preserves his brick home and grounds and is open to visitors in season. Its exhibits tell the story of the 1781 ride and of early farm life in Woodford County. Jouett's milling and distilling are early chapters in a county now known for its bourbon distilleries.
